answers.question: How much capital funding could Berkeley redirect to streets?

resolution.scope: CIP Fund 501 and Measure FF only. Other capital funds (sewer, storm water, zero waste, parks tax, state and county transportation funds, internal service funds) are not yet assessed here.

answers.short_answer: From Measure FF, nothing beyond the adopted plan without a vote of the people. From CIP Fund 501, at most $2,946,000 of FY2027-FY2028 money, and only by deferring or cancelling every other project the fund pays for; 88% of its FY2027 money ($10,412,200) already goes to paving. A one-time amount from unspent carried-over appropriations may exist but cannot be measured from public records; its ceiling at June 30, 2025 was $11,568,647.

interpretation.text: The capital money Council could redirect to paving without voters is small relative to the paving gap: the City estimates PCI 70 needs about $8 million a year more, while fund 501's non-paving capital is $1,473,000 a year, mostly repairs to existing City buildings.
interpretation.counterargument: This covers only fund 501 and Measure FF. Other capital funds, unspent carryovers, the General Fund itself and delivery-cost savings are not assessed here and could change the total.

answers.question: Could Measure FF money pay for more street paving?
answers.short_answer: No, not without a vote. Voters fixed the split at approximately 45% streets, 15% sidewalks, 30% safety and 10% environmental, and the ordinance bars Council from altering it. The adopted program already puts 45.6% of Measure FF ($42,119,935 of $92,282,816) into street rehabilitation.

cite.quote: 60% for streets and sidewalks, of which roughly three quarters (45%) will be for streets

facts.label: Council cannot change the allocation without voters

cite.quote: the City Council shall not be authorized to impose the special tax for the following two years
is projected to yield $16,651,651 in revenues

calculations.label: Street rehabilitation share of the five-year Measure FF program

interpretation.text: Measure FF is not a source of additional paving money; it is already allocated to paving at the share voters set.
interpretation.counterargument: The split is "approximately" 45%, so a modestly larger street share might be defensible; and once the citywide PCI reaches 70 the allocation stops being required. Neither changes the answer for FY2027-FY2028.

missing_evidence.needed: June 30, 2026 Measure FF balance (the first rate covered 18 months of collections)

answers.question: How bad are Berkeley's streets, beyond the average PCI?
answers.short_answer: The average hides most of it. In the 2024 inspection the network averaged PCI 56, but 88.75 centerline miles (42% of the network) were below PCI 50 and 33.99 miles were below 25. The City projects an average of about 62 by 2038 with Measure FF, but publishes no projection of how many streets will still be below 50. The adopted plans treat 22.61 miles of currently-below-50 streets over five years.

cite.quote: The updated Pavement Management Program showed that the City's overall average PCI is 56.

interpretation.text: Reaching a network average of 60 or 62 is not the same as eliminating failed streets; the measure that matches Measure FF's goal is the mileage below PCI 50.
interpretation.counterargument: Treating the worst streets first costs more per point of average PCI (the City shows about one point lower in 2038), so a lower failed-street count can mean a lower average; both measures are needed.

answers.question: What does the $139.3 million streets figure include?
answers.short_answer: It is the five-year (FY2027-FY2031) Streets capital budget, not a two-year one: the paving plan ($96,336,212), Measure FF street rehabilitation ($42,119,935), bridge maintenance and Harold Way placemaking add to exactly $139,356,147. The two-year FY2027-FY2028 Streets amount is $58,211,462.

interpretation.counterargument: FY2029-FY2031 are planned amounts and may change; the two-year figure is the only one with appropriations behind it.
